connections.note: Part A handles the technical objections to the cosmological argument (“what caused God?”, Hume’s and quantum mechanics’ challenges to causation, composition, god of the gaps, Krauss’ universe from “nothing”). Part B picks up where the god-of-the-gaps discussion left off, digging out the scientism behind it, and relies on Part A’s results — e.g., Gerson’s point that “maybe there’s no explanation” can’t answer an offered explanation.

The hierarchical (per se) causal series of the Aristotelian proof returns in the brute-fact reply: a regress of laws, like a regress of instrumental causes, needs a first member with underived power. The closing account of demonstration uses the Aristotelian proof as its example (change can’t be refuted by any future experience, since every experience is a change).

The Neo-Platonic proof’s starting point — that things are composite — is contrasted with Paley-style “complexity”: any composite thing, even a pebble or a drop of water, will do. Its conclusion, an absolutely simple One, is why the complex-designer objection misses.

The Augustinian proof’s defense of the necessity and objectivity of logical and mathematical truths is what breaks Hume’s Fork and the “science or conceptual analysis” dichotomy; natural theology’s truths are placed alongside them.
The Thomistic proof’s God, whose essence is his existence, is the God who is not “a being” among others but subsistent being itself — the key to answering “one god further.”

The principle of sufficient reason defended in the rationalist proof is invoked repeatedly: against the claim that ultimate explanation is unavailable, against treating the laws as brute facts, and in the account of how the premises of a demonstration are defended.

Divine simplicity, immutability, immateriality, and necessity underwrite the contrast between the God of classical theism and the limited pagan gods, and between a self-explanatory ground and a brute fact.

Feser’s replies to Mackie and Rowe build directly on chapter 6’s account of omnipotence (no power to do contradictions), goodness, evil as privation, whether God must create the best world, and God’s love; the hiddenness reply reuses the same greater-good reasoning.

The introduction promised that chapter 7 would show the most common objections to be feeble and overrated, and that the real debate is not atheism vs. theism but among theists of different stripes. Part B makes good on both: the popular objections are dismantled one by one, and the reply to “the philosophers’ God isn’t the believer’s God” repeats the point that the serious remaining debate is among theists.

This module supplies the diagnostic toolkit for the capstone: sort any objection by whether it refutes itself, attacks a caricature, or applies the wrong standard, then return to a specific premise. It also contains the book’s concluding account of what it means for the five proofs to be demonstrations.

quiz.q: How does Feser define scientism?
options: The practice of using controlled experiments to test hypotheses
The view that science and religion address separate, non-overlapping questions
The view that science alone gives genuine knowledge, so legitimate philosophy is only what is implicit in science
The view that scientific theories are merely useful tools for prediction
quiz.explanation: Scientism is a philosophical thesis about the scope of knowledge, not the practice of science itself. The last option describes instrumentalism, one of the interpretive questions Feser says philosophy must settle.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is scientism self-refuting when taken strictly?
options: Because the claim that only science yields knowledge cannot itself be established by scientific method, and science rests on presuppositions only an extrascientific standpoint could justify
Because scientific theories are constantly revised and so never yield certainty
Because scientists disagree among themselves about fundamental physics
Because science cannot yet explain the origin of the universe
quiz.explanation: The self-refutation lies in the thesis’s own status: it is a philosophical claim that science cannot establish. Revisability and current gaps are not Feser’s argument; he explicitly avoids god-of-the-gaps reasoning.

quiz.q: What goes wrong if the defender of scientism responds by counting philosophy as part of “science”?
options: Science would lose its predictive power
Philosophy would have to adopt mathematical methods
Nothing — this is Feser’s preferred resolution
The thesis becomes trivial, and it can no longer exclude natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas regarded as a science
quiz.explanation: This is the second horn of the dilemma. A definition of science broad enough to include philosophy has no non-arbitrary way of excluding natural theology, so scientism can no longer serve its purpose of dismissing it unheard.

quiz.q: The example of engineers treating airline passengers as average weights is meant to show that…
options: physics is less reliable than engineering
a feature’s absence from an abstract description may result from the method’s design rather than from the feature’s nonexistence
human beings are ultimately reducible to physical quantities
averages never correspond to any actual individual
quiz.explanation: The engineers’ data say nothing about meal preferences because the method looks only at weight. Likewise physics leaves out qualities, meanings, and purposes by design. The last option is a detail of the example, not its point.

quiz.q: What point does Feser take from Bertrand Russell about physics?
options: Physics will eventually explain consciousness
Physics gives only the abstract mathematical structure of events, not the intrinsic nature of what has that structure
Physics proves that the universe had a beginning
Physics shows that causation is merely constant conjunction
quiz.explanation: Russell, no friend of theism, stressed physics’ abstractness. Feser adds that since structure must be the structure of something, physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes.

quiz.q: Why does the Humean view of laws of nature give no support to the idea that science provides the ultimate explanation of the world?
options: Because Hume believed laws were decrees of God
Because on this view laws are abstract objects outside the physical world
Because on this view laws describe the essences of things, which must already exist
Because on this view laws only summarize regularities, telling us that a pattern holds but not why
quiz.explanation: Humean laws redescribe rather than explain. The other options describe the Cartesian-Newtonian, Platonic, and Aristotelian views, each of which fails for a different reason.

quiz.q: Feser compares Rosenberg’s argument from the success of science to which argument?
options: Metal detectors find metal better than any other method, so metallic objects are probably all that is real
Telescopes see farther than eyes, so eyes are unreliable
Maps are useful, so the territory must be flat
Medicine cures diseases, so all illness is physical
quiz.explanation: The metal-detector parody has exactly the same form: from unmatched success at detecting one kind of thing to the claim that probably nothing else exists.

quiz.q: Rosenberg says critics of scientism happily trust their cardiologists but cry “scientism” when their metaphysics is scrutinized. What is Feser’s reply?
options: Critics of scientism should stop relying on cardiologists
Cardiology is not really a science
Trusting a method within its domain doesn’t commit you to its having no limits — like trusting metal detectors without thinking they alone detect physical things
Metaphysics can also be tested by cardiology
quiz.explanation: The charge of inconsistency assumes that trusting science anywhere requires trusting it as the sole source of knowledge. Insisting that science, unlike metal detectors, covers all of reality would beg the question.

quiz.q: Feser’s analogy of the student who takes only easy courses and boasts of his GPA is aimed at which claim?
options: That philosophy has made no progress since Aristotle
That natural theology is a kind of science
That scientific theories are revisable
That even if science can’t answer everything, it answers everything worth knowing, as shown by its consensus and technology
quiz.explanation: If only predictable, consensus-yielding questions count as scientific, science’s success is guaranteed trivially and says nothing about the value of the questions it excludes. The claim is also itself philosophical.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say the claim that any non-scientific inquiry is mere “conceptual analysis” refutes itself?
options: Because conceptual analysis always yields false results
Because the claim itself is neither a conceptual truth nor something natural science could support — like Hume’s Fork
Because Ladyman and Ross are not scientists
Because neuroscience has disproved conceptual analysis
quiz.explanation: The dichotomy falls between its own tines. Feser adds that appealing to neuroscience would beg the question, since whether such sciences are our only source of knowledge about cognition is what is at issue.

quiz.q: What role do the truths of logic and mathematics play in Feser’s critique of scientism?
options: They show that all knowledge is ultimately empirical
They prove that God exists directly
They are knowledge that fits neither tine of Hume’s Fork, being necessary (unlike science) and objective (unlike mere conceptual analysis)
They show that philosophy is just a branch of mathematics
quiz.explanation: Logic and mathematics are counterexamples to the science-or-conceptual-analysis dichotomy, and Feser places the conclusions of natural theology in the same category.

quiz.q: Which thinkers does Feser say essentially held that the fundamental laws of nature are an unexplained brute fact?
options: J. L. Mackie and Bertrand Russell
Aristotle and Aquinas
Descartes and Newton
Plato and Plotinus
quiz.explanation: Feser cites Mackie’s *The Miracle of Theism* and Russell’s debate with Copleston. Descartes and Newton held a theological view of laws; Aristotle and Aquinas grounded laws in natures.

quiz.q: What is the point of the image of a book on a shelf held up by brackets that are then let go in midair?
options: If the fundamental laws are unexplained, the higher-level laws that depend on them cannot really explain anything either
Physical objects need support to stay in place
The universe had a beginning in time
Laws of nature change over time
quiz.explanation: A regress of laws is like a hierarchical causal series: without a self-explanatory first member, borrowed explanatory power has no source. That is the third problem with the brute-fact view.

quiz.q: What does Feser call the most important problem with the objection that a designer would be more complex than the universe?
options: Dawkins misread Paley
Complexity is subjective
The five proofs agree that a complex cause would need a cause, which is exactly why they conclude the first cause is absolutely simple
Probabilistic reasoning is always unreliable
quiz.explanation: Feser gives three replies (no appeal to complexity, no appeal to probability, and this one), and calls this the most important: the objection presupposes a composite God that the proofs explicitly rule out.

quiz.q: Which starting point would serve the Neo-Platonic proof but would never be used by Paley or an Intelligent Design theorist?
options: The human eye
A pebble or a drop of water
The bacterial flagellum
A pocket watch
quiz.explanation: The Neo-Platonic proof needs only something composite; it doesn’t care how many parts or how precisely arranged. Paley’s argument needs intricate, function-serving complexity.

quiz.q: According to Feser, the deeper flaw in the “one god further” objection is that it…
options: ignores the historical influence of polytheism
overlooks that some pagans were monotheists
fails to count all the gods correctly
commits a category mistake by treating the God of classical theism as one member of a class of beings called “gods”
quiz.explanation: The first reply is that there are arguments for God and none for Zeus; the deeper one is that God is in no genus, shares no essence with other gods, and is being itself rather than a being.

quiz.q: In Feser’s anti-Euclidean analogy, if physical space turned out to be non-Euclidean, what would follow about Euclidean triangles?
options: They would turn out to have imperfectly straight sides
They would be identical to non-Euclidean triangles
They would simply not be instantiated, rather than being imperfectly straight
They would become merely conceptual
quiz.explanation: The claim that Euclidean triangles have crooked sides doesn’t even make sense. Likewise, if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God is one more nonexistent god — the objection misdescribes what is being denied.

quiz.q: According to the Catholic teaching Feser cites, which truth about God is knowable only through divine revelation?
options: That God is omnipotent
That God is omniscient
That God is the cause of the world
That God is a Trinity
quiz.explanation: Omnipotence and omniscience can be known both by reason and by revelation; the Trinity only by revelation. It is the same God known by different routes.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a defense and a theodicy?
options: A defense is religious; a theodicy is philosophical
A defense shows that evil is logically compatible with God; a theodicy tries to say why God actually permits the evils that exist
A defense addresses moral evil; a theodicy addresses natural evil
There is no difference; the terms are synonyms
quiz.explanation: Feser offers a defense, which suffices to rebut the objection. He notes older Thomistic works used “theodicy” to mean natural theology in general, but not that the terms are synonyms in the modern sense.

quiz.q: How does Feser answer Mackie’s claim that God could have created free creatures who always freely choose good?
options: He grants that such a world is possible but argues it couldn’t contain goods like forgiveness, mercy, courage, and compassion, which presuppose actual evil
He denies it, following Plantinga, on the grounds that any free creatures would sometimes sin
He argues that free will is an illusion
He argues that this is the best of all possible worlds
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly says the theist need not take Plantinga’s route, and in a footnote he rejects Leibniz’s best-possible-world claim. His point is that certain moral goods require evil.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think Rowe’s evidential argument poses no challenge to the book’s proofs?
options: Because animals do not really suffer
Because Rowe’s example is fictional
Because suffering is always a punishment for sin
Because believing there is no greater good is rational only if we lack independent reason to think a good God exists, and the proofs supply such reason
quiz.explanation: Rowe concedes a hidden greater good is possible. Given independent proof of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God, we have reason to think such a good is actual. To challenge the proofs, the argument would first have to refute them.

quiz.q: Why is Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument a nonstarter against Aristotle’s theism?
options: Because Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover contemplates itself and takes no notice of us, so it doesn’t seek a personal relationship
Because Aristotle believed God was obvious to everyone
Because Aristotle denied that God exists
Because Aristotle held that humans lack free will
quiz.explanation: The argument assumes God intends a personal relationship with us. A theism without that assumption is untouched, so the argument fails as a completely general case for atheism — though Feser himself holds that God does seek such a relationship.

quiz.q: What does Feser use Thomas Nagel’s admission that he hopes there is no God to show?
options: That all atheists are intellectually dishonest
That the charge of motivated reasoning can be made against critics of theism too, so motives settle nothing
That Nagel secretly believes in God
That scientism is a religious belief
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly says not all atheists are dishonest. The point is symmetry: since bias can run either way, only examining the arguments can decide.

quiz.q: Why can’t the Aristotelian proof’s premise that change occurs be overturned by future empirical inquiry?
options: Because it is known a priori, independently of experience
Because physics has confirmed it
Because any possible future experience would itself be an instance of change
Because Aristotle defined change that way
quiz.explanation: The premise is empirical in a sense (so the proof isn’t a priori), but it can’t be empirically refuted: we might show some particular change unreal, never that all change is. This is part of what makes a demonstration more secure than a scientific inference.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the dilemma Feser poses for scientism.
shortAnswer.model: Scientism is either self-refuting or trivial. Taken narrowly, the claim that only science gives knowledge is not itself scientifically established, and science rests on presuppositions (a mind-independent, orderly world knowable by our faculties) it cannot justify without circularity; it also needs philosophy to interpret its results. So the thesis undercuts itself. Taken broadly — counting philosophy as “science” — it becomes vacuous and can no longer exclude natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas regarded as a science more certain than physics. Either way it cannot justify dismissing natural theology unheard.
rubric: States both horns: self-refuting vs. trivial
Explains why the thesis isn’t scientifically established
Mentions science’s philosophical presuppositions and/or need for interpretation
Explains why the broad version lets natural theology in and defeats scientism’s purpose

shortAnswer.q: Why can’t physics give a complete description even of physical reality?
shortAnswer.model: Physics deliberately restricts itself to what can be described mathematically, and so predicted and controlled. Everything qualitative — colors as experienced, sounds, thoughts, purposes, meanings — falls through its net by design, as the airplane engineers’ weight calculations leave out passengers’ tastes. Its silence about such features is not evidence that they don’t exist. Moreover, as Russell stressed, physics gives only abstract structure, not the intrinsic nature of what has the structure; since there can’t be structure without something structured, physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes.
rubric: Methodological restriction to the quantitative
The engineers analogy or equivalent point that silence isn’t denial
Russell’s structure vs. intrinsic nature point
The inference that structure implies something beyond structure

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct the argument from the success of science and explain why Feser thinks it fails.
shortAnswer.model: Premise: science’s predictive power and technological applications are unmatched. Conclusion: what science reveals is probably all that is real. It fails because success at capturing one aspect of reality doesn’t show there are no others — just as metal detectors’ unmatched success at finding metal doesn’t make it probable that only metal exists. Physics succeeds precisely because it attends only to the mathematically modelable. Replying that science, unlike detectors, covers the whole of reality begs the question. The same fallacy underlies demands for metaphysics’ predictions — like asking for gardening’s metal-detecting record.
rubric: States the two-step argument accurately
Gives the metal-detector parody
Explains why success within a domain doesn’t show the domain is everything
Notes the question-begging reply

shortAnswer.q: Give Feser’s three objections to the view that the fundamental laws of nature are a brute fact.
shortAnswer.model: (1) It contradicts the principle of sufficient reason, defended in chapter 5. (2) It is ad hoc: its only motivation is to avoid arguments like the five proofs, since the Humean and quantum-mechanical challenges to PSR fail, and one can’t answer an offered explanation by saying there might be none (Gerson). (3) If the fundamental laws are unexplained, no higher-level law explains anything — like a shelf resting on brackets that are let go in midair. A regress of laws needs a self-explanatory terminus that imparts explanatory power without deriving it, which only something purely actual, simple, whose essence is existence, and necessary can be.
rubric: Conflict with PSR
Ad hoc / no independent motivation (Gerson point is a plus)
Higher-level laws lose explanatory power; shelf/brackets image
Connects to hierarchical series and a self-explanatory terminus

shortAnswer.q: Why does the objection that a designer would be more complex than the universe miss the five proofs?
shortAnswer.model: It targets Paley-style design arguments, which argue probabilistically from intricate, artifact-like complexity to a designer. The five proofs (1) don’t appeal to complexity in that sense — a pebble would do for the Neo-Platonic proof; (2) don’t appeal to probability — they are strict demonstrations about hierarchical causes operating now, so talk of a more parsimonious alternative misses them; and, most importantly, (3) agree that a complex cause would need a cause, which is precisely why they conclude that the first cause is absolutely simple. Nothing the atheist proposes as the terminus of explanation is simple in this way.
rubric: Identifies the target as design arguments (Paley/ID)
No appeal to complexity (pebble example)
Demonstration vs. probabilistic reasoning; hierarchical vs. linear
The proofs conclude to an absolutely simple cause — the key point

shortAnswer.q: Explain why Feser calls the “one god further” objection a category mistake, and why the point doesn’t depend on theism being true.
shortAnswer.model: The objection treats God as one member of the class “gods,” like Zeus or Thor. But the God of classical theism belongs to no genus (which would make him composite), shares no essence with others (which would distinguish his essence from existence), and is the purely actual source of all causal power — not a being but subsistent being itself. The pagan gods are limited beings with bodies, moods, parents, and beginnings. Treating God as one more god is like treating triangularity as one more triangle or the Form of the Good as one more good thing. Even if Euclid or Plato were wrong, Euclidean triangles would just be uninstantiated, not crooked; similarly, even if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God is one more nonexistent god.
rubric: States what the category mistake is
Gives at least two ways God differs from pagan gods (simplicity, essence = existence, pure act, not a being)
Uses the triangle or Form-of-the-Good analogy
Explains why the point holds whether or not theism is true

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser answer Mackie’s logical problem of evil?
shortAnswer.model: He offers a defense, not a theodicy. Mackie’s second premise — an omnipotent being faces no limits and a good being eliminates all the evil it can — fails twice. Omnipotence doesn’t extend to contradictions, so if some goods logically require evils, God can’t have the goods without them. And a good being doesn’t eliminate every evil it can, because some goods presuppose evils (the parent who won’t cancel homework). Against Mackie’s point that God could create free beings who always choose good, Feser grants it is possible, even with morally significant choices, but denies such a world could contain all the goods of ours: forgiveness and mercy require wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires misfortune; sacrifice requires loss. Mackie later conceded the logical argument fails.
rubric: Defense vs. theodicy
Omnipotence and contradictions
Goodness doesn’t require eliminating every evil (homework example)
Grants Mackie’s free-will point but cites goods that require evil
Mackie’s later concession (bonus)

shortAnswer.q: What is Rowe’s evidential argument and how does Feser respond?
shortAnswer.model: Rowe argues that a perfect being would prevent suffering preventable without losing a greater good or permitting something as bad; probably some suffering is like that (the fawn burned in a forest fire, suffering for days); so probably there is no such being. He concedes we can’t prove there is no greater good. Feser replies that believing there is no greater good is rational only if we lack independent reason to think a good God exists — and the proofs, plus the arguments for God’s attributes, supply it. Since Rowe grants a hidden good is possible, independent proof of God gives reason to think it actual. So the argument can’t challenge the proofs without first refuting them independently. Our ignorance is also expected: if there is an afterlife, an endless good could outweigh finite suffering, and we can no more grasp it than a child can grasp adulthood.
rubric: Accurately states Rowe’s argument and the fawn
Notes Rowe’s concession
Independent-evidence reply
The argument can’t challenge the proofs without refuting them first
Afterlife / child-adult point and that its possibility suffices for a defense

shortAnswer.q: Identify the two assumptions behind the divine hiddenness argument and summarize Feser’s case against each.
shortAnswer.model: (1) If God existed his existence would be obvious. Schellenberg grounds this in God’s desire for personal relationship, but not all theists hold that (Aristotle’s aloof Unmoved Mover), and even for those who do, the argument doesn’t touch the attributes the proofs establish. Regarding God’s love, as with evil, independent proof of a loving God implies there is a greater good in his not being more obvious. Hick’s epistemic distance is overstated but contains a kernel: finite minds and free will allow error. (2) God’s existence isn’t obvious to most people. In fact most people historically and today are theists of some kind; the weakness of ordinary people’s reasons no more makes God hidden than laymen’s weak grasp of science makes science hidden; most experts historically held God knowable by argument; and intellectuals who reject God on incompetent objections have no standing to call him hidden.
rubric: States both assumptions
Aristotle counterexample and limited scope of the argument
Greater-good reply parallel to Rowe
Hick’s epistemic distance and its kernel of truth
Most people are theists; layman-science analogy

shortAnswer.q: What does “demonstration” mean for classical theists, and why doesn’t widespread disagreement show that the proofs fail?
shortAnswer.model: A demonstration is a deductively valid argument from premises that are certain, their certainty shown by metaphysical analysis. It is more secure than scientific inference because it isn’t probabilistic or a best-explanation inference, and its premises can’t be overturned by future observation, since all observation presupposes them (any future experience would itself be a change). But nothing about such arguments implies everyone will immediately see their force, or that no hard work is needed to defend them. Disagreement doesn’t show failure: much criticism is ill-informed, and skeptics apply a double standard — arguments for materialism or against free will aren’t said to fail merely because they have critics (Putnam’s point). What a demonstration requires is that it can be defended against every objection.
rubric: Definition: valid deduction from certain premises
Two ways it differs from scientific inference
Change-example or equivalent
Controversy ≠ failure; double standard
Standard: defensible against all objections

shortAnswer.q: How would you respond, briefly and humanely, to a friend who says their suffering makes belief in God impossible?
shortAnswer.model: First, listen and acknowledge that what happened is truly evil — not secretly good. Admit honestly that you don’t know why it happened; Feser offers only a defense, not an explanation of particular evils, and argues we should expect not to see God’s reasons. If and when your friend wants to think it through, share gently that the reasons for believing in God don’t depend on explaining this event; that some of the deepest goods — mercy, courage, compassion — exist only where there is suffering; and that if God is real and good, this suffering is not the last word. Avoid clichés like “everything happens for a reason,” and don’t use their pain as a debate.
rubric: Listening and acknowledgment come first
Honest admission of not knowing why (defense, not theodicy)
Gentle statement of the core points only when welcome
Avoids glibness and clichés

flashcards.back: The view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge. Feser: a key New Atheist premise with no good arguments for it and decisive ones against it.
(1) Self-refuting or trivial; (2) science can’t give a complete description of reality; (3) laws of nature can’t give a complete explanation; (4) the argument from science’s success has no force.

flashcards.front: First horn of the scientism dilemma
flashcards.back: Self-refuting: “only science gives knowledge” isn’t a scientific result, and science’s presuppositions can be justified only from outside science.

flashcards.front: Second horn of the scientism dilemma
flashcards.back: Trivial: stretching “science” to include philosophy makes the thesis empty and lets natural theology count as science (as Aristotle and Aquinas held).
A mind-independent objective world; law-like regularities in it; our intellect and senses can discover and describe them.
Treating passengers as average weights is useful, but it’d be absurd to conclude they have no meal or movie preferences. Physics’ silence about qualities is likewise built into its method.
Physics gives the abstract mathematical structure of events but is silent about the intrinsic nature of what has the structure — so there must be more to reality than physics says.

flashcards.front: Aristotelian view of laws — why no ultimate explanation
flashcards.back: Laws describe how things act given their natures, so they presuppose the things and can’t explain their existence (or the universe’s).

flashcards.front: Cartesian-Newtonian view of laws — why no help to scientism
flashcards.back: Laws are shorthand for God’s ordering of the world, so God does the real explaining.

flashcards.front: Humean view of laws — why no ultimate explanation
flashcards.back: Laws merely summarize regularities: they say that a pattern holds, not why. They redescribe rather than explain.

flashcards.front: Platonic view of laws — why no ultimate explanation
flashcards.back: We’d still need to explain why a physical world participates in the laws at all, and in these rather than others.
Itself a philosophical, not scientific, claim — and false, since it violates PSR.
(1) Science’s predictive and technological success is unmatched; (2) so what science reveals is probably all that is real.
Metal detectors find metal better than anything else, so metal is probably all that exists. Same form as the argument from science’s success — and obviously bad.
Searches for his keys only where the light is and concludes they can’t be anywhere else — the scientism mindset.
Taking only easy classes and boasting of your grades: counting only predictable, consensus-yielding questions as “science” guarantees its success trivially.
All objects of inquiry are relations of ideas or matters of fact. Self-refuting: it is neither. Modern version: science or mere conceptual analysis (Ladyman and Ross).

flashcards.front: Logic and mathematics vs. Hume’s Fork
flashcards.back: Necessary (unlike science) and objective (unlike mere conceptual analysis) — they fall between the tines, as do the truths of natural theology.

flashcards.front: The thief and the squad car
flashcards.back: The scientism advocate, with oceans of knowledge he can’t account for, demanding credentials from natural theology is like a thief caught with the loot demanding the police prove they own their cruiser.
(1) Violates PSR; (2) ad hoc — motivated only by avoiding the proofs; (3) leaves higher-level laws with no real explanatory power.
Explaining by laws that rest on an unexplained law is like letting go of a shelf’s brackets in midair and expecting the book to stay up.

flashcards.front: Three replies to “a designer would be more complex”
flashcards.back: (1) The proofs don’t appeal to complexity; (2) they aren’t probabilistic and concern hierarchical causes now; (3) most importantly, they agree complex things need causes — so the first cause is absolutely simple.
It’s a perfectly good starting point for the Neo-Platonic proof (anything composite), but no design theorist would use it — showing the proofs aren’t design arguments.
There are at least five demonstrations for the God of classical theism and no one offers arguments for Zeus, so there’s no inconsistency.
Category mistake: God isn’t a member of the genus “gods” (he is simple), shares no essence with others (essence = existence), and is being itself, not a being.
“I just go one step further and say triangularity itself has crooked sides.” Confuses the standard with an instance. If Euclid were wrong, Euclidean triangles would be uninstantiated, not crooked.

flashcards.front: Philosophers’ God vs. believers’ God — two replies
flashcards.back: (1) Irrelevant: if the proofs work, atheism is false. (2) False: e.g., Catholic teaching identifies them, and ordinary believers believe in the same God less technically (like ball-and-stick atoms).
Defense: shows evil is compatible with God. Theodicy: explains why God actually permits evil. Feser offers a defense.
That an omnipotent being has no limits and a good being eliminates all evil it can. Omnipotence excludes contradictions; some goods presuppose evils.
Forgiveness and mercy (require wrongdoing), courage (danger), compassion (misfortune), sacrifice (loss of a good).

flashcards.front: Feser vs. Plantinga on free will
flashcards.back: Feser grants Mackie that God could make free creatures who never sin; he argues such a world still couldn’t contain goods like forgiveness and courage.
A fawn burned in a lightning-caused fire, suffering for days before dying — Rowe’s example of apparently pointless suffering.
“No greater good” is rational only without independent reason to believe in a good God; the proofs supply that reason, and Rowe grants a hidden good is possible.

flashcards.front: The two assumptions of the hiddenness argument
flashcards.back: (1) If God existed, his existence would be obvious to most people; (2) it isn’t. Feser rejects both.
Overstated (the world isn’t religiously ambiguous; believers do evil without doubting God), but a kernel of truth: finite minds and free will give us a long leash in what we think.
Rejecting an argument because of the arguer’s motives. Irrelevant to validity and soundness — and it cuts both ways (Nagel’s cosmic authority problem).
Skeptics treat any objection to a theistic argument as showing it fails, but not arguments for materialism or against free will (Putnam).
A deductively valid argument from certain premises, whose certainty is shown by metaphysical analysis — not probabilistic, and not overturnable by future observation.

teachBack:
**Challenge:** Explain to a science-minded friend who has never read Feser why “science doesn’t need God” is not an argument against the five proofs — in under four minutes, without using the words “metaphysics,” “Aristotelian,” or “actuality.”

You must: (1) separate science from scientism in one sentence; (2) use either the metal detector or the airplane engineers; (3) show why “only science gives knowledge” can’t be proved by science; and (4) finish by naming the one thing that *would* count against a proof (a false premise or an invalid step).

**Round two:** In two minutes each, give a one-line answer and a one-paragraph explanation for “Who designed the designer?” and “You’re an atheist about Zeus — just go one god further.” Use no analogy twice.

**Round three (the hard one):** Role-play with a partner who plays someone whose close relative has recently died. Your goal is *not* to win. Practice listening, acknowledging, saying “I don’t know why,” and only then — if your partner invites it — explaining the difference between a defense and a theodicy and why some goods require evil. Ask your partner afterward: did anything I said feel glib?

**Check yourself:** Could your friend now restate the scientism dilemma in their own words? Did you ever accidentally argue from a gap in current science? Did you claim to know why God permits a particular evil? If yes to either of the last two, revisit the summary sections on scientism’s problems and on Mackie and Rowe.
videoPrompt: Audience: thoughtful beginners, including skeptics raised on popular science. Overview the second half of Chapter 7 of Feser’s Five Proofs. Emphasize, in order: (1) scientism — only science gives knowledge — is self-refuting or empty, and physics captures measurable structure by design (airplane engineers treating passengers as average weights; the metal detector); (2) brute-fact laws explain nothing, like a shelf whose brackets are let go in midair; (3) “who designed the designer?” and “one god further” attack a caricature: the proofs reach an absolutely simple God who is being itself, not one more god (triangle vs. triangularity); (4) evil: defense vs. theodicy, goods like forgiveness and courage that require evil, Rowe’s fawn; (5) hiddenness, motives, disagreement. Correct two myths: rejecting scientism means rejecting science; Feser claims to know why each evil happens. Tone: warm, clear, fair to critics, humane about suffering.
